title: Pear is brown inside: when it is overripe and when it is spoiled

seo.title: Pear brown inside: overripe or spoiled?
seo.meta_description: A pear can turn brown and soft first around the core as it becomes overripe. Watery breakdown, mushiness, fermented odor, or mold are reasons to discard it.
seo.search_intent: Distinguish internal browning from advanced overripeness in pears and more serious breakdown or spoilage.

excerpt: A pear can begin browning around the core after it has ripened too far or exceeded its useful storage life. A small firm-to-soft brown area may reflect overripeness, but watery, collapsing, moldy, or fermented-smelling tissue is a reason to discard the fruit.
content_html:
A pear can feel decent on the outside and still reveal brown flesh around the seeds. Many European pears ripen from the inside outward, so the core can move past peak quality before the peel looks obviously bad.

UC Davis describes core breakdown as a senescent disorder: fruit held too long can develop brown, soft tissue in and around the core. Advanced maturity, delayed cooling, and extended storage increase the likelihood.

A little brown does not always mean rot

If the browning is limited, the remaining flesh has a normal texture and sweet pear aroma, the fruit may simply be very ripe. Trim the unappealing section and eat the rest immediately rather than storing it again.

An overripe but otherwise sound pear is often better in sauce, puree, oatmeal, or baking than as crisp slices.

When the center is actually breaking down

Core breakdown can progress until brown tissue becomes very soft and separates easily from healthier flesh. UC Davis also describes watery breakdown, where affected pear tissue loses structure, becomes water-soaked, and may release juice when cut.

If the inside is watery, slimy, collapsing, fermented-smelling, moldy, or leaking from deteriorated tissue, discard the pear. At that point the issue is no longer just a cosmetic brown patch.

Texture draws the practical line

What you findWhat to do
Small brown area, flesh still soundTrim and eat immediately
Soft core but no off odor, damage limitedVery ripe; use now if the remaining fruit is sound
Water-soaked or collapsing tissueDiscard
Mold or fermented odorDiscard

Browning can begin as a sign that a pear has gone too far in ripening; loss of structure, liquid, and off odor show that the problem has progressed. Cutting the fruit in half tells you much more than the peel alone.

faq.question: Why is a pear brown inside but okay on the outside?
faq.answer: The core can become overripe or develop storage-related breakdown before the exterior shows an obvious problem.

faq.question: Can I eat a pear with a little brown around the core?
faq.answer: If the brown area is small, there is no mold or off odor, and the rest of the flesh is sound, trim it away and use the pear immediately.

faq.question: When should a brown-inside pear be thrown away?
faq.answer: Discard it when the tissue is water-soaked, very mushy, slimy, moldy, leaking, or has a fermented or rotten odor.
